head:
Seniors · Masters · Power

Why power declines before strength

At 50 or 60, many people say they feel less sharp before they say they feel weaker. This article checks whether that impression has any basis: do speed and jumping decline before maximal strength, at what age, why, and what difference does it make? It demonstrates the answer in six steps, then gives the real level of certainty.

The question

Imagine two tests on the same day. In the first, you lift the heaviest load you can once, or squeeze a dynamometer as hard as you can: that is maximal strength. In the second, you stand up from a chair five times as fast as possible, or jump as high as possible: that is power, strength multiplied by the speed at which you apply it. A muscle can be strong and slow, or less strong and very quick.

Most fitness assessments stop at the first test. Yet what you do in daily life looks more like the second: getting up from an armchair, catching yourself when your foot snags, speeding up to cross the road, sprinting again in sport. These movements require strength, but above all strength fast.

Hence the question. If movement speed declines before maximal strength, a strength test alone can reassure you for years while something has already been lost. So we need to know by how much, from what age, why, and whether anything can be done about it.

The question

Does muscle power (strength applied fast) really decline earlier and faster than maximal strength? If so, from when, why, what does it signal for your daily life, and what should you measure and train as a result?

What is at stake

The first stake is independence. Getting up from a low chair, climbing stairs, catching yourself when your foot snags: these movements require power, not only strength. Someone who can still lift a heavy load slowly may lack the speed to straighten up when they lose their balance. The article “How the body ages”, covers falls, fractures and the different slopes of decline; I do not repeat it. This one follows a single slope, the steepest, and how to see it.

The second stake is measurement. If power declines earlier than strength, monitoring that measures only strength misses the earliest signal, during the period when it is easiest to act. The third is the performance of veteran athletes, the “masters”: you can train seriously and still lose speed. The fourth is health: cohorts associate low leg power with more hospitalisations, mobility limitations and deaths (association, not cause: see step 5).

This question cannot be left unanswered because the loss is silent: you notice it the day a movement no longer works. “I am less sharp” is a subjective and late signal. The studies below let us see whether a number can show it earlier.

The demonstration

The reasoning goes from the most general to the most precise: the groups (step 1), the movement itself (step 2), the starting age (step 3), the causes (step 4), what this signals (step 5), then the objections, the counter-examples and what can be done (step 6).

Step 1In the groups studied, power declines faster than strength

Claim: in healthy older people, leg power declines roughly two to three times faster per year than isometric strength.

Skelton and colleagues compared 50 healthy men and 50 healthy women, evenly spread between 65 and 89 years old. They measured isometric strength (pushing against a fixed resistance, without moving) and the power of the leg extensors (the force developed when pushing fast). Result: strength declines by about 1 to 2% per year, power by about 3.5% per year. The gap between the two is clear in men (p = 0.0001, a result very unlikely to be due to chance) and is not in the women of the sample (p = 0.08).1

Between 65 and 89, leg power declines roughly two to three times faster than leg strength

Solid bar: low end of the strength range (1%). Light bar: up to the high end (2%). Annual rates given by the authors, estimated from people of different ages measured once (cross-sectional study). Source: Skelton et al., Age and Ageing, 1994 (abstract).1

What this means

Two caveats: the gap is established in men, not in the women of this group, and these are group averages, not your trajectory.

Another cohort points the same way. In the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, upper-body strength and power begin to decline around age 40 in both sexes. In men, power declines by about 10% more than strength. In women, no significant difference appears, with only 4.6 years of follow-up on average against 9.6 years in men.2

Where this leads. These measurements mix strength and speed in a single number. We need to look at the movement itself: how fast force rises when you push as hard and as fast as you can.

Step 2What goes first is the force you can produce right away

Claim: the ability to develop force quickly, at the start of the movement, declines more than maximal strength.

Researchers measure this with the rate of force development (RFD): how many newtons you gain per millisecond when you push as fast and as hard as possible. The higher this rate, the faster your force arrives. It is what matters when you have a fraction of a second to catch yourself, not the force you would reach after three seconds.

Two studies compare men of different ages. The first brings together 32 healthy men aged 21, 40 and 71 on average: at 71, isometric leg strength is 46% lower than at 21, and the rate of force development 64% lower. Jump heights (squat jump and countermovement jump) and standing long jump length are lower in the 71-year-olds than in the other two groups (p < 0.001).5 The second compares 14 men aged 27 with 14 men aged 67, all physically active: the maximal strength of the older men is about 45% lower, their maximal rate of development about 50% lower, and their rate of development in the first 30 milliseconds about 76% lower.6

The more you look at the start of the movement, the bigger the gap with young people

Percentages given by the sources (gap of the older group compared with the younger one), rounded by them. Two small samples, cross-sectional comparison: orders of magnitude. Sources: 1999 study of 32 men, titled “Maximal and explosive force production capacity and balance performance in men of different ages”; Granacher et al., Aging Clinical and Experimental Research, 2010.5,6

What this means

In both studies, maximal strength is about 45% lower in the older men, and what is measured at the start of the movement is much lower still, up to 76% over the first 30 milliseconds. The older men can therefore still push hard, but they take longer to get there. In the second study the older men were active: the delay is therefore not only an effect of sedentary behaviour. A maximal-load test says little about this delay.

An older study compares men aged 22-24, 41-43 and 71-77 (five per group). Compared with the 41-43-year-olds, the oldest have isometric strength about 30% lower, a rate of force development about 47% lower and a squat jump about 50% lower.4 A review chapter on Finnish masters sprinters aged 17 to 82, second-hand and without sample sizes, gives the same pattern: countermovement jump from 52 to 23 cm (about 56% lower) against about 36% lower for maximal squat load.14

Where this leads. Two independent clues point the same way. What remains is the starting age: at 75, it is a subject for geriatrics; at 45, it is a subject for you, now.

Step 3It starts in midlife and speeds up with age

Claim: power declines from the forties onward, and the annual rate of decline doubles, then doubles again, between the twenties and the sixties.

The best type of evidence is following the same people over time. A 2023 study measured maximal power, strength and velocity in 489 adults (311 men, 178 women), aged 19 to 68 at baseline, then ten years later. Maximal power declines each year by about 0.6% in young men (20-40), by 1.1 to 1.4% from 40 to 60 and by 2.2 to 2.4% beyond 60 (for some groups, p is 0.053, just above the 0.05 threshold).7

The annual rate of power loss doubles, then doubles again, with age

Solid bar: low end of the range. Light bar: up to the high end. Absolute maximal power (in watts), ten-year follow-up of 489 adults. Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, April 2023 (abstract).7

What this means

The decline does not wait for retirement: it is already measurable in adults aged 40 to 60, at a rate close to double that of 20-40-year-olds, then it doubles again in those over 60. An annual percentage adds up from one year to the next: at 2% per year, power falls by about a fifth in ten years (approximate calculation by the author). These rates concern absolute power; the weight that increases with age further accentuates the decline in power relative to body weight, which the authors note.

Cross-sectional cohorts place the onset in the same spot. In the Copenhagen Sarcopenia Study (1,305 people aged 20 to 93), relative power (per unit of body weight) declines after 40 in both sexes, mainly because absolute leg power declines while body mass index rises.9 In a European cohort of 9,320 people aged 60 to 103 and 586 adults aged 20 to 60, relative power in the 30-second sit-to-stand test declines by about 0.05 W/kg per year between 30 and 50 (not significant), then by 0.10 to 0.13 W/kg per year between 50 and 80 (watts per kilo is power relative to body weight).8

In 240 masters athletes aged 35 to 91, jump power declines by about 0.20 W/kg per year (about 2 W/kg per decade) and jump height by about 0.27 cm per year (about 2.7 cm per decade), both per-decade figures being derived from the regression coefficients.10 These are selected athletes: the decline is seen even in highly trained people.

Where this leads. The loss is early and accelerating. Why does it go faster than the loss of strength? The answer lies in the muscle, and it is not as simple as it is made out to be.

Step 4Why: fast fibres, nerve drive and speed, with disagreements

Claim: several mechanisms add up, and their relative weight changes with age and from person to person. They explain why movement speed declines more than strength.

Power is strength multiplied by speed. There are therefore two ways to lose it: producing less force, or producing it more slowly. Muscle contains two main families of fibres: slow (type I), which are enduring, and fast (type II), which produce a lot of force quickly and tire sooner. It is the fast ones that do jumps and sprints.

Lexell and colleagues examined the whole thigh muscle of 43 previously healthy men who had died, aged 15 to 83. Age-related atrophy begins around age 25 and speeds up. It comes mainly from a loss of fibres, with no predominance of one type, and for a smaller part from a reduction in fibre size, especially of the fast ones.11 The answer “fast fibres disappear first” is therefore not demonstrated as such: what is established is that their size decreases more.

The second mechanism is nerve drive. Reid and colleagues followed healthy older adults and older adults with mobility limitation for about three years. Leg power declines comparably in both groups (about 8.5% and 8.8%). In healthy adults, maximal strength and muscle size are maintained; what decreases is neuromuscular activation, with a reduced contraction velocity. With mobility limitation, strength also declines (about 5.9%), with muscle loss.12

In healthy older adults, power declines over three years while strength holds

The source gives a range of 8.5 to 8.8% for power without assigning each value to a group: both bars are drawn at 8.65% (middle of the range). For healthy adults, the source states that strength is “maintained” without quantifying it: baseline line at zero. Source: Reid et al., European Journal of Applied Physiology, 2014 (abstract).12

What this means

This is the most direct illustration of your question: in these healthy adults, a maximal strength test would have shown nothing over three years while power had declined by about one twelfth. With mobility limitation, strength and power decline together. Two profiles, not a single rule.

The other sources do not settle it as clearly. In 565 adults aged 65 and over followed for 8 years, about 95% of the average decline in relative power comes from a decline in power per kilo of leg muscle, and about 5% from muscle loss.20 In a study of 129 adults, the best link with maximal knee power is the speed of torque development under electrical stimulation (R² of 0.69 in men, 0.57 in women), with voluntary drive being only weakly linked in women and not in men: the loss would come mainly from the muscle.13 In the 2023 follow-up, the early decline in power follows that of strength, while the late decline involves both strength and velocity.7

The results partly contradict each other: nerve drive in Reid, muscle properties in Wrucke. What emerges is that the loss of power has several causes, that their share varies with age, and that muscle mass alone does not explain it.

Where this leads. The causes are multiple. What remains is to see whether low power is linked to what matters to you: mobility, hospitalisation, survival.

Step 5What power signals: mobility, hospitalisation, survival

Claim: low leg power is associated with mobility limitations, hospitalisations and, in men, higher mortality, beyond age and other factors.

In Skelton, power relative to body weight is linked to the time to get up from a low chair and to the step height one can climb, whereas strength relative to body weight is linked only to chair-rise time.1 In the European cohort of 9,320 people aged 60 to 103, 18% of women and 16% of men had a mobility limitation. Relative power below 2.1 W/kg (women) or 2.6 W/kg (men) clearly distinguishes those who have one: the likelihood is multiplied by 10.6 and 14.1 (odds ratios adjusted for age). Retain a very strong link, not the exact value.8

García-García and colleagues followed 1,928 participants in the Toledo Study for Healthy Aging. They measured relative leg power with five chair rises, relative to body weight, and sorted participants into groups (thirds of power, plus a group unable to do the test). Over 6.3 years on average, the very low power group has more deaths than the high power group: a risk ratio of 2.3 in men and 2.9 in women, adjusted for age. After adjusting for physical activity, body mass index, education, depression, associated diseases, disability and grip strength, it remains 2.1 in men (confidence interval 1.1 to 3.8) and 1.6 in women (0.8 to 3.2, not significant).15

Very low leg power goes with more deaths, partly beyond age and grip strength

The last group (women, 1.6) is not significant: its interval of 0.8 to 3.2 contains 1, hence the light bar. Risk ratios supplied by the source, drawn from zero. Source: García-García et al. (including Alcazar), Journals of Gerontology A, 2021 (abstract).15

What this means

In men, very low power remains linked to a risk of death about twice as high even after accounting for grip strength, general fitness, diseases and age. This suggests that power provides information that grip strength does not. In women, the association disappears after adjustment: the data allow us neither to confirm nor to reject it.

Where this leads. A coherent body of clues is not proof. The next step looks for what contradicts it.

Step 6The objections and the counter-examples

Claim: “power goes before strength” is true on average and in several groups, but not everywhere or for everyone, and several figures are more fragile than they look.

Objection 1: the samples are small and mix different ages

Studies with 5, 10 to 12, 14 or 100 people are small, and most compare people of different ages at the same moment: age, generation and lifestyle get mixed together. Hence the orders of magnitude. The two longitudinal follow-ups (489 adults over 10 years, 565 over 8) point the same way.7,20

Objection 2: this is not the case for everyone

In Skelton, the gap is not significant in women (p = 0.08); in Metter, no significant difference in women; in García-García, the link with mortality disappears in women after adjustment.1,2,15 This does not prove there is no gap: these studies could not show it (small samples, short follow-up in Metter).

Objection 3: the counter-example of masters sprinters

Hendrickse and colleagues followed 24 Finnish male masters sprinters (aged 48 to 85 at baseline, 61.9 on average) from 2002 to 2012. Their jump power declines by 9.5% in ten years, but their knee extensor strength by 21.0%, more than double, and their 60-metre time increases by 14.2%. The authors attribute the loss of power to the loss of strength, not to muscles that have become slower. Fibre size and type and capillaries do not change significantly, so the cause of the loss of strength remains unknown, and years of training are not linked to the size of the decline.16

In masters sprinters, strength declined more than jump power over ten years

24 masters men, aged 48 to 85 at baseline, measured ten years apart. The heights are proportional to the source values (means, with standard deviations of 5.7, 20.4 and 12.4 points); the 60-metre time increases when speed falls. Source: Hendrickse et al., Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2025.16

What this means

This result overturns the formula: in these sprinters, strength goes faster than jump power. It is consistent with the 2023 follow-up (early on, power follows strength), but it shows that the order of losses depends on the person, the measure and the movement. These figures are not those of the general public: 24 men, highly trained.

There is a benchmark for running speed: 70 finalists at European veterans' championships, filmed over 100 metres, lose about 5 to 6% of speed per decade in men and 5 to 7% in women.17 Hendrickse's 60-metre time increases by 14.2% in ten years, which is a speed about 12% lower (1 divided by 1.142, derived calculation), double the benchmark. One possible explanation, not demonstrated here: following the same people shows a larger decline than comparing different ages.

Objection 4: “relative” power mixes muscle and weight

Power relative to body weight also declines because weight goes up.9,7 Part of the “relative power loss” of a person who gains weight is not muscle loss: track your absolute power (or your performance on a movement) and your weight.

Objection 5: association is not cause, and the feeling is not measured

No source read here shows that low power causes hospitalisation or death: a sick person, sometimes without knowing it, gets up more slowly. Adjusting for reported diseases reduces this bias without eliminating it. No study read here measures the feeling of “feeling slow before feeling weak” either: it is a plausible hypothesis based on step 2, not a result.

What remains uncertain

I could not open the review by Reid and Fielding (2012) or the meta-analysis by Straight and colleagues (2016): none of their figures are used. I also cannot say at what age a power test becomes more useful than a strength test for you: this has not been compared directly in what I read.

The answer to the question

Does power decline earlier and faster than maximal strength? On average, in several groups over 40, yes: about 3.5% per year for leg power against 1 to 2% for strength in 65-89-year-olds; a rate of force development up to 76% lower over the first 30 milliseconds while maximal strength is about 45% lower; maximal power that loses 0.6% per year at 20-40, 1.1 to 1.4% at 40-60, 2.2 to 2.4% beyond; and, in healthy older adults, about 8.5 to 8.8% of power lost in three years while strength held.

The answer is not universal: several studies could not confirm the gap in women, strength declined more than jump power in 24 masters sprinters, and the causes vary between studies. Level of certainty:

  • Solid (several studies, two multi-year follow-ups): power declines from the forties onward, at a rate that speeds up with age; force produced at the start of the movement is much lower than maximal strength in older people compared with young people.
  • Probable (studies of varying quality): at group level, power declines faster than strength in men; low power is linked to more mobility limitations, hospitalisations and, in men, deaths, including after adjustment for grip strength.
  • Uncertain: why (nervous or muscular, strength or speed), and whether this holds as much in women.
  • Not established: that improving your power reduces hospitalisations or mortality; that people feel slower before they feel weaker; that power goes “before” strength in every individual.

In one sentence: the decline in power is early and fast at group level, it is not always visible with a strength test alone, but it is not an individual rule.

What to put in place

The data do not allow us to promise protection, but they do support measuring the right movement and training speed along with strength.

  1. Add a fast movement to your strength tests.A timed chair rise (five repetitions, the test used in the Toledo cohort) or a vertical jump gives information that maximal load does not.15 The tests on this page give the starting point; their protocol is below.
  2. Read both numbers together.If your strength holds but your fast movement slows, that is the profile described in Reid. This is my practical reading, not a diagnostic rule.12
  3. Repeat the same measurements under the same conditions, every 6 to 12 months.Same chair, same shoes, same warm-up, same time of day. This frequency is an editorial recommendation: no source read sets it. Also watch your weight: it distorts relative power (objection 4).
  4. Strengthen the legs while aiming for speed in the push phase.In a randomised trial of 57 adults aged 65 to 94 with mobility limitation (74.2 on average), training three sessions a week for 12 weeks at 70% of maximal load (leg press and leg extension) increased power comparably whether the push was fast or slow, compared with a group that stretched. The fast group nonetheless produced about 2.3 times (extension) and 2.8 times (press) more power during the sessions.18 Conventional strength training therefore already raises power.
  5. Do not expect miracles from “explosive” training.A meta-analysis of 19 trials (1,055 people over 60) compares fast-push and traditional training: a small to moderate effect on the physical performance battery (standardised difference of 0.27) and on the timed up-and-go test (0.35), low-quality evidence, with very uncertain effects on the rest (chair rises, walking speed, balance).19 A pilot trial of 12 people saw velocity at maximal power increase by 3 to 18% with fast training against about −1 to +1% with slow training, with no established functional advantage: not to be generalised.3
  6. Build up gradually.First fast movements without impact (chair rise, leg push), then light jumps. Editorial precaution, with no source read.

Chest pain, dizziness, a recent fall or joint pain on exertion justify medical advice before speed or jump tests.

What these figures do not say
  • Several studies are small (5 to 14 people per group) and cross-sectional: they compare different ages at the same moment. Averages do not give your trajectory.
  • Masters sprinters are highly trained men; the links with hospitalisation and death are associations; several figures come from abstracts or a review chapter, flagged in the sources.

Frequently asked questions

My strength is good: should I still worry about my power?

Not necessarily, but the studies show older adults whose strength held while power declined by about 8.5 to 8.8% in three years.12 Measuring a fast movement lets you see it; it does not mean you have a problem.

Should I train “explosively”?

The trials read show comparable power gains with conventional strength training and with fast pushing, with a possible small advantage of the fast approach on some tests, of low quality.18,19

Does this concern women too?

Power declines in them too in the ten-year follow-up.7 That it declines faster than strength is not established: several studies found no significant gap.1,2

Does a veteran athlete escape this decline?

No: the masters in the ten-year follow-up lost jump power, strength and speed despite their years of training.16 What we do not know is how much greater the decline would have been without training.
